summary.text: Since every factor is a prime at least 2, a product different from 1 forces the associated-prime set to be nonempty, so it has a maximum. For any associated prime \(p\), if \(m-p\) were composite it would have a prime divisor \(q\le\sqrt{m-p}\le\sqrt m\), forcing \(p\equiv m\pmod q\) contrary to the defining avoidance condition; hence the maximum and its complement are prime, and applying this at each \(n\) gives Goldbach.

full_proof.text:
Let \(\lfloor\sqrt M\rfloor\) denote the integer square root of a natural number \(M\). For \(M>0\), define \(GB(M)\) to be the finite set of natural numbers \(p\le M/2\) such that

1. \(p\) is prime;
2. \(\lfloor\sqrt M\rfloor<p\); and
3. for every prime \(q\le \lfloor\sqrt M\rfloor\),
   \[
   p\bmod q\ne M\bmod q.
   \]

For \(M=0\), set \(GB(0)=\varnothing\). Thus the sequence in question is
\[
a(n)=\prod_{p\in GB(2n)}p,
\]
with the usual convention that the product of the empty set is \(1\). (The definition separately assigns the value \(1\) when \(2n=0\), which agrees with this convention.)

This residue formulation is also the stated Goldbach-association condition. Indeed, if \(p\in GB(M)\) and \(q\le\lfloor\sqrt M\rfloor\) is prime, then \(q<p\). Since \(p\) and \(q\) are prime, \(q\nmid p\). Consequently, \(q\nmid p(p-M)\) is equivalent to \(q\nmid(p-M)\), and the latter is equivalent to \(p\not\equiv M\pmod q\).

We first prove the key fact about every member of \(GB(M)\).

**Lemma.** If \(p\in GB(M)\), then \(M-p\) is prime.

**Proof.** Membership in \(GB(M)\) gives
\[
p\text{ prime},\qquad \lfloor\sqrt M\rfloor<p,
\qquad p\le \left\lfloor\frac M2\right\rfloor,
\]
and
\[
p\bmod q\ne M\bmod q
\quad\text{for every prime }q\le\lfloor\sqrt M\rfloor.
\]
In particular, a prime \(p\) satisfies \(p\ge2\). The inequality \(p\le\lfloor M/2\rfloor\) implies \(2p\le M\), and hence
\[
M-p\ge p\ge2.
\]
We show that \(M-p\) has no divisor between \(2\) and its integer square root. Suppose, to the contrary, that a natural number \(d\) satisfies
\[
2\le d\le\lfloor\sqrt{M-p}\rfloor
\quad\text{and}\quad d\mid M-p.
\]
Let \(q\) be the least prime factor of \(d\). Since \(d\ge2\), the number \(q\) is prime, divides \(d\), and satisfies \(q\le d\). It follows that \(q\mid M-p\). Moreover,
\[
q\le d\le ig\lfloor\sqrt{M-p}\big\rfloor
   \le ig\lfloor\sqrt M\big\rfloor,
\]
because \(M-p\le M\). Thus the defining residue condition for \(p\in GB(M)\) applies to this prime \(q\).

On the other hand, \(q\mid M-p\) gives \((M-p)\bmod q=0\). Since \(p\le M\), natural-number subtraction satisfies
\[
M=(M-p)+p.
\]
Reducing this equality modulo \(q\), we obtain
\[
M\bmod q=p\bmod q,
\]
contrary to the defining condition for \(GB(M)\). Therefore no such divisor \(d\) exists.

A natural number \(N\ge2\) is prime precisely when it has no divisor \(d\) with
\(2\le d\le\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor\): if \(N\) were composite, its least prime factor would be at most \(\sqrt N\). Applying this criterion to \(N=M-p\) proves that \(M-p\) is prime. \(\square\)

We next record how the condition \(a(n)\ne1\) ensures that the associated set is nonempty. For any finite set \(S\) of natural numbers all of whose elements are at least \(2\),
\[
\prod_{x\in S}x=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad S=\varnothing.
\]
The reverse implication is the empty-product convention. For the forward implication, if \(S\) were nonempty, choose \(x\in S\). Then \(x\ge2\), while \(x\) divides the product over \(S\). If that product were \(1\), then \(x\mid1\), forcing \(x\le1\), a contradiction.

Now fix \(n\ge3\) and suppose \(a(n)\ne1\). Put
\[
M=2n,
\qquad S=GB(M).
\]
Because \(n>0\), we have \(M\ne0\), so the defining expression for the sequence is exactly
\[
a(n)=\prod_{p\in S}p.
\]
Every member of \(S\) is prime, hence is at least \(2\). If \(S\) were empty, the preceding product would equal \(1\), contrary to the hypothesis. Therefore \(S\) is nonempty.

The set \(S\) is finite: by definition it is a subset of
\(\{0,1,\ldots,\lfloor M/2\rfloor\}\). Hence its maximum exists. Let
\[
m=\max S.
\]
Then
\[
m\in S
\quad\text{and}\quad
k\le m\quad\text{for every }k\in S.
\]
Applying the lemma to the membership \(m\in GB(M)\) gives
\[
M-m=2n-m\quad\text{is prime}.
\]
This establishes the claimed local conclusion: \(GB(2n)\) is nonempty, its maximum \(m\) exists, belongs to the set, dominates all its elements, and has prime complement \(2n-m\).

It also shows explicitly that this maximum provides a Goldbach partition. Since \(m\in GB(2n)\), the number \(m\) itself is prime and
\[
m\le \left\lfloor\frac{2n}{2}\right\rfloor=n\le2n.
\]
Thus natural subtraction has no truncation issue, and
\[
(2n-m)+m=2n.
\]
Both summands are prime, so \((2n-m,m)\) is a Goldbach partition of \(2n\).

Finally, assume the global hypothesis
\[
a(k)\ne1\qquad\text{for every }k\ge3.
\]
Let \(n\ge3\) be arbitrary. Applying the local argument to this \(n\) yields the maximum \(m\in GB(2n)\), with both \(m\) and \(2n-m\) prime and with
\[
2n=(2n-m)+m.
\]
Therefore every even integer \(2n\) with \(n\ge3\) is the sum of two primes. This is precisely the stated form of Goldbach’s conjecture, and the same argument simultaneously supplies the asserted specific partition using \(m=\max GB(2n)\).
